lines: Four o'clock. The bench is warm. I am on time.
I fold the paper in four. Then I mostly look at the sea.
The cat on the wall and I have an understanding. We both sit.
That gull has been standing on one leg since three. Admirable.
Crossword, nine across: a long rest. Siesta. Too easy.
Up the hill, the church bell says four. Down here, nobody minds.
The cane goes here, the paper goes there. Now I am settled.
Biscuit passed this morning and inspected my shoes. Approved.
A gull just walked past me like it owned the promenade. It may.
My wife says I come down for the view. I come for this bench.
The ginger cat has chosen the warm end of the wall. Wise cat.
I walked down from the church. Seven minutes. Eight with waving.
Ten down: a small sweet pastry. Marcel would know at once.
I hum the same tune every afternoon. The gulls know it by now.
Someone at the café is playing an accordion. Slowly. Perfect.
I have read this page twice. It improves with the sea behind it.
Three gulls, one chip. They are being very polite about it.
Afternoon is the best hour. I say that about every hour.
My crossword pencil gets a little shorter every year. Good years.
The palms are doing their slow wave. I wave back, a little.
I count the white houses. Forty-one. Yesterday it was forty-one.
Odile walked by and said I look rested. I am a professional.
A sparrow just looked at my crossword. It had no suggestions.
I knew the man who planted these cypresses. Very tall now. Both.
Seven letters, a kind of tree. Cypress. They are right there.
I bring a biscuit for myself and half a biscuit for the gulls.
Léo ran past three times. I am counting for his records.
This bench faces west. By six it will be the best seat in town.
When I was young I sat on the other end. Now I prefer this one.
A good afternoon has no plans in it. This one is very good.
The paper, a pencil, a peppermint. Everything a man needs.
I read the weather twice. Sun both times. Lovely consistency.
There is a gull who comes every day at half past four. Like me.
The zinc roofs go silver about now. I wait for it.
I learnt the harmonica last winter. Three songs. All slow.
Henri says I nap. I say I am resting my eyes on the view.
The kiosk sells me one peppermint a day. We are both loyal.
Every cobblestone down the hill knows my cane by now.
The cat jumped down to say hello and jumped back. Very formal.
Twelve across: hello, in French. I wrote bonjour with a flourish.
A child gave me a shell this morning. It lives in my pocket now.
Biscuit once sat with me a whole crossword. Fine company.
My knees and I agree: the bench is the right decision.
The church is up there, the sea down here. My walk is in between.
I bring the same paper back tomorrow if the crossword is hard.
Look, the café awning has been lowered. Shade for everyone.
The cat is asleep in a perfect circle. I admire the geometry.
I am reading a book about gardens. I do not garden. I read.
That bougainvillea is louder pink than yesterday. Good for it.
Four letters, a sweet spread. Miel. My wife will be proud.
I take the long way down. There is a geranium I like to visit.
Someone is whistling near the fountain. I am whistling back.
This hour the sea is the colour of a blue shirt I once had.
I tip my hat to everyone. My arm gets good exercise.
A gull landed on the next bench. We are both enjoying our benches.
The cat has rolled over. That is as excited as it gets here.
I keep a small notebook of birds. Today: gull, gull, sparrow.
The bread was warm at noon. I am still pleased about it.
Thirty years of this view with Henri. Still not tired of either.
Marcel waved a napkin at me. That means the tarte is good.
I drew the fountain in the margin. The fountain looks surprised.
That little cloud has not moved in an hour. A cloud after my heart.
I sit very still and the sparrows come closer. A fine trade.
Afternoons by the church are quiet. Afternoons here are quieter.
The cat on the wall blinked at me slowly. I blinked back. Friends.
I brought my reading glasses and my other reading glasses.
Lucie rang her bell at me. I lifted my cane. Our little hello.
The lavender pot by the café smells best around now. Lean in.
I have finished the crossword. Now I can just sit. The best part.
Gulls in the afternoon are lazier. I approve of their schedule.
Here is my method: sit, look, sit a bit more. Then look again.
On the way down a lady gave me a fig from her tree. Delicious.
The shade of that palm reaches my shoes at five. Like a clock.
I read three pages and one gull. Very productive.
Théo has walked past with a baguette like a trophy. Quite right.
My grandson taught me to fold a paper hat. I wear it in summer.
Is that music from the café? A waltz. My feet are tapping.
The wall cat has a tail like a question mark. I have no answer.
Every afternoon I learn one new name of a flower. Today: freesia.
The sea is doing nothing in particular. I join it.
A gull feather blew onto my paper. I am using it as a bookmark.
I always save the easiest clue for last. A small treat.
The light on the white houses is like milk in coffee now.
Odile told me who is courting whom. I have forgotten. Charming.
When the bench is warm and the paper is dull, that is happiness.
A tip for you: walk slowly. You see twice as much.
I sang in the church choir for forty years. I hum the low parts.
The string lights are waiting. So am I. We are in no hurry.
Five down, a word for content. Happy. I filled it in quite fast.
I am learning Norwegian. Today's word is koselig. I feel it now.
My granddaughter is teaching me chess by letter. I lost by post.
Practising my watercolours. Everything comes out a little blue.
I proposed to my wife at that fountain. She said oui very fast.
Forty-three years ago I danced under those string lights. Badly.
I am memorising a poem, one line each afternoon. Six to go.
My first ice cream was from that kiosk. Pistachio. Still is.
Learning to whittle. This is either a bird or a small potato.
I am practising card tricks. Pick a card. No, the other hand.
Our wedding photo was taken right here. The bench looked younger.
Knitting lesson number four. The scarf is now as long as a sock.
I taught my son to ride a bicycle on this promenade. He wobbled.
The year it snowed, the whole town came out to look. Just once.
Practising Italian from a little book. Buongiorno, bench.
I am learning to juggle. Two oranges, so far. Three is ambitious.
Here I first heard my grandson laugh. A very good noise.
Practising my bird calls. A sparrow answered. Or it was a squeak.
I learnt to swim at seventy off those rocks. Slowly, but I did.
Each day I learn one star name. Tonight I will test myself.
I am practising patience. The bench is an excellent teacher.
The summer fête of '89, Henri won the cake. He shared it with me.
Learning the ukulele. My fingers are older than the strings.
My wife taught me to make tarte tatin. I am still practising.
I learnt to tie a bow tie for my daughter's wedding. Still can.
Practising my signature. It was getting lazy in retirement.
The first time I saw the town, it was this exact light.
Writing letters with a fountain pen again. My hand remembers.
I am learning the names of the clouds. That one is a cumulus.
Practising a waltz step in my head. My feet will follow later.
Learning to bake bread. My loaf this morning was nearly round.
My daughter took her first steps toward that palm. Then sat.
I am trying to whistle with two fingers. Not yet. One day.
Origami, lesson six. This is a crane. It is a little shy.
The café gave me free coffee the day I retired. A fine morning.
Practising my sketching. Today: the kiosk. It came out lovely.
I learn one new joke a week. This week's is about a baguette.
Once a whole band played under these palms. We all sang along.
My wife and I shared our first café crème at table three.
Practising calligraphy. My capital A is very proud of itself.
The day the fountain was switched on, I was the first to splash.
I am learning to read music. The notes look like little birds.
My brother and I raced up the hill as boys. He won. I laughed.
Learning to play the spoons. The café says I keep good time.
I once found a lucky coin under this bench. I still carry it.
Today I practise sitting up straight. It lasts about a minute.
The lamplighter used to wink at me. Now the lamps light themselves.
I am teaching myself to draw hands. Mine look like mittens.
My grandson and I flew a kite here once. It flew. We cheered.
Practising my tango with the cane. Very small steps.
A neighbour taught me a card game. I win when she is kind.
I learnt to make jam at sixty. Apricot. Everyone got a jar.
Practising the accordion at home. My wife wears earmuffs, kindly.
The first summer here I painted our shutters sea blue.
I am learning to say thank you in nine languages. Takk is my best.
Henri taught me pétanque on that gravel. I still aim too long.
My best birthday was a picnic on this promenade. Seventy candles.
Practising a little song for my wife. Her birthday is Sunday.
I am learning to spin a coin on its edge. Ten seconds today.
The year the palms were planted, they were shorter than me.
Learning the cello at eighty. The cello is being very generous.
My son caught his first fish off those rocks. Then let it go.
Practising my handstand. In my mind. It is excellent there.
Learning to name the bells up the hill. The small one is Marie.
The café once named a sandwich after me. Ham, butter, patience.
Practising the art of the long lunch. Today I got to four.
A summer storm once kept six of us under the café awning. Grand.
Learning to plant tomatoes on my balcony. Three are blushing.
My wife and I counted shooting stars from this bench. Eleven.
Practising my best hello. Warm smile, small bow. Bonjour, you.
I learnt to dance the farandole at the fête. The whole street did.
Learning sign language for hello and thank you. Very handy.
My grandson built a sandcastle here with a moat. We were proud.
Practising mental arithmetic. Two peppermints plus one. Lovely.
I learnt to make a daisy chain from a girl of six. Expert teacher.
Learning to paint the sea. It keeps changing. So do I.
The first evening the string lights went up, we all clapped.
Practising my reading without glasses. The big letters are fine.
My daughter learnt to read on this bench. The cat book, twice.
Learning to make a proper omelette. Fold, not roll. Nearly there.
Practising gratitude. Sun, bench, bread. Easy today.
Henri and I once carried a piano down this street. Singing.
Learning the steps of the hill by heart. One hundred and twelve.
I practise walking without the cane to the corner. Then hello, cane.
My wife and I first held hands by that cypress. Still there.
Today I am learning one new street name. Rue des Lilas. Pretty.
Practising my skipping stone wrist, ready for the beach later.
Every afternoon I learn a neighbour's name. Today: Camille.
I am practising humming in tune. The fountain keeps me honest.
My first job was carrying bread up the hill. I ate the corners.
Learning to take photographs. My thumb is in most of them. Charming.
The day my grandson was born, I bought the whole café a coffee.
The bougainvillea goes purple-grey now. It is thinking about tomorrow.
My geraniums will want water at seven. I will be there at seven.
The jasmine by the church gate opens about now. I can smell it here.
Henri's lemons look like little lamps in this light.
The rosemary gets repotted tomorrow. I have said so since Tuesday.
My father planted a fig by our door. It still feeds the whole lane.
The lamps came on one by one. I counted. Fourteen, then I lost track.
A slow evening. The best kind. Then the hill, then the kettle.
My granddaughter calls on Sundays. She asks after the tomatoes first.
Ten more minutes. The bench and I have an understanding.
The church bell says nine soon. My knees say whenever you like.
That oleander by the kiosk has outdone itself this year.
The basil is in the window. It likes to watch the street, like me.
I left the shutters open so the lavender can see the stars.
Bread, the paper, a word with the lemon man. Tomorrow is full.
The cypresses go black first. Then everything else follows politely.
Four pots of mint on my step. I gave one away. Still four. Mint.
From this bench you can hear the café stacking the little cups.
I walk home the long way at this hour. Past the good hedges.
The palms are just shapes now. Very elegant shapes.
My mother pressed flowers in her prayer book. I still find them.
The bougainvillea gets a trim soon. Only a small one. It is shy.
My lemon tree has three lemons. I have names for two of them.
Up by the church the swifts will be settling. Down here, me.
A cushion would be nice. Then again, this bench has never minded.
The roses on my wall are the same ones my brother planted. Stubborn.
Look at the fountain. It goes silver when the lamps come on.
I promised the tomatoes a feed tomorrow. A promise is a promise.
Odile waved with her whole arm. I waved with my cane. Both count.
Blue sky, yellow windows. Somebody painted this, surely.
Night-scented stock. You only notice it if you sit very still.
My grandson says I sit like a statue. A happy statue, I hope.
Plan for tomorrow: nothing hurried. A fine plan. I make it daily.
The kiosk is closing its shutters. Click, click. A nice sound.
The hill is gentler in the evening. Or I am. One of us.
Henri's newspaper is folded. That means the day is finished.
My little olive tree leans toward the sea. It knows what it likes.
Every window is a different yellow. I have a favourite. Third one.
The light is going blue on the zinc roofs. Very Paris of it.
I bring my cane for the hill and keep it for the company.
That lamp by the fountain flickers on last. Every evening. Thorough.
Seventy-nine summers on this hill. Each one better watered.
My geraniums are red, pink and one surprise. I like the surprise.
Sit long enough and the whole promenade says goodnight to you.
The bougainvillea drops a petal on my knee. A small hello.
My sister sends seeds in her letters. This year: marigolds.
I water at dawn and admire at dusk. The plants seem to approve.
Tonight I will read two pages and sleep before the third.
The café umbrellas are folding up like flowers at night.
A neighbour left apricots on my step. I will leave figs on hers.
Look how the palms hold the last of the light. Like a tray.
A visit to the nursery tomorrow. Just to look. I always buy something.
The air smells of jasmine and warm stone. My favourite recipe.
Henri and I have shared these benches for forty years. Nearly.
As a boy I caught fireflies by the church. They are still there.
The lamps make little moons on the paving. One each.
My hydrangeas went blue this year. I did nothing. They decided.
This is the bench for blue hour. The other one is for mornings.
My grandchildren come in August. I am growing strawberries for them.
A little cool now. Just right for the walk up.
The lemon tree on my terrace flowered twice. Showing off.
The music from the café reaches just this far. Lovely.
From here the whole town looks like a cake with candles.
I keep a chair by the rosemary. We have long talks.
Tomorrow, the market. Peaches, if they are good. They will be.
My father whistled to his tomatoes. I hum. Times change.
The last swallow went home. I will be right behind it.
The terracotta pots are still warm. They kept the day for later.
The church cat sleeps in my thyme. It smells wonderful, the cat.
Someone's window has a lemon tree in it. Good for them.
On Thursday I swap cuttings with the baker's mother. A fine trade.
Look up. First star. Over the church, as it should be.
Same bench, same lamps. Somehow it never gets old.
Evening is when the flowers stop posing and just smell.
I have three watering cans. One for each mood. All good moods.
The bougainvillea on the post office is nearly to the roof now.
I sit, the town lights up around me. Very considerate.
The sweet peas want tying up. They are getting ideas.
The evening is so quiet you can hear the lemons ripening.
My first garden was a single tin can of marigolds. Still my best.
Henri says his bench has the better view. Mine has me on it.
Blue hour, warm stone, a good cane. A man needs little else.
Morning glories closed up for the night. Me soon, too.
The planters on the promenade are all in flower. Who is so clever?
My daughter painted my door green. The geraniums look even redder.
Every evening I pick one lamp to walk home by. Tonight, that one.
The fountain sounds softer at dusk. Or my ears are just content.
I keep my seed packets in a biscuit tin. Some are older than Léo.
Up the hill, water the pots, then bed. A perfect itinerary.
Bonsoir, lemon trees. Bonsoir, bougainvillea. See you at seven.
Six o'clock bell. I sit down on the third stroke.
The shutters go gold one by one. Left to right, always.
My wife says I come down for the light. She is right.
The fountain sounds softer in the evening. Or I listen better.
Forty years of evenings on this promenade. Not one the same.
The clock is two minutes fast. It likes to be early for sunset.
My cane gets the end of the bench. It has earned a rest too.
The café awning has gone the colour of apricots.
I counted the blue tiles on the fountain once. I lost count happily.
My father sat here too. He also pretended to read.
Paper folded, hat tipped back. That is the evening posture.
The cypresses are getting long shadows. Very distinguished.
Henri says golden hour. I say it is just the hour. The best one.
Anouk, my granddaughter, calls this my office.
Margot and I courted on this very bench. Bench number five.
A swallow just went under the café awning. Home for supper.
I like a bench that faces west. A man knows where he stands.
The zinc roofs up the hill have turned to copper.
Shutters open, geraniums out. Someone is cooking onions.
Every evening the fountain gets a little gold coin of sun.
Margot will ask what I saw. I will say: all of it.
Lucie went by on her bicycle. The bell was in a good mood.
I sat down for five minutes. That was a while ago.
The church clock and the town clock agree tonight. Rare.
My knees and I came down slowly. The view waited.
Look at the whitewash. It blushes every evening.
Grandson asked what I do down here. I said: supervise.
The palm by the post office is waving hello. Or goodbye.
A pigeon has been sitting next to me for a while. Good company.
I brought the crossword. I am letting the sun do it.
The terracotta pots on the steps glow like little lanterns.
Yusuf and Biscuit, punctual as the bell. Biscuit leads.
In my day we had one bench and four of us. Now look.
This light is old friends with my face. It knows the wrinkles.
Margot packed me a peach. I am saving it for the pink part.
The café chairs lean together. Gossiping, I expect.
My bench, my hat, my evening. A small kingdom.
Someone on the hill is practising the piano. Slowly. Nicely.
The fountain has a new coin in it. Somebody made a wish.
The shutter on the blue house is half open. Like a wink.
When my son was small he raced me to this bench. He won.
The clock face is catching the sun. It looks pleased with itself.
Evening, says Henri. Evening, I say. That is our conversation.
There is a breeze that smells of lemon trees and bread.
A good bench is warm from the afternoon. This one is perfect.
Léo ran past three times. I think he was going somewhere.
Camille waved. Léo waved harder. Families are like that.
My cane is resting against the armrest. We are both off duty.
The promenade tiles go from white to honey about now.
Margot's mother had shutters that exact green. Fine taste.
I tip my hat to the joggers. They have no time to tip back.
The sea is very busy being pretty. I am very busy watching.
The awnings are rolling up. The day is folding its napkin.
On Sundays Anouk sits with me and tells me everything. Lovely.
I have read this page three times. The sun keeps interrupting.
A bench is the best seat in any theatre. And free.
The stone of the fountain is warm. I touched it on the way.
They painted this bench in my thirties. Still holding up. Both of us.
I tell the time by the café. Clinking cups means six.
The fountain spouts and the gulls bow. Every evening, a ballet.
The church tower has gone the colour of good marmalade.
Someone has hung washing on the hill. It is waving at me.
My grandfather planted one of those cypresses. The tall one.
Marcel is lighting the candles. One, two, three, four. Splendid.
Shadow of my hat is longer than me now. Quite a hat.
A man needs one hour a day with nothing to do. This is mine.
The church bell rings once for half past. Polite of it.
Henri brought the good newspaper. I brought the good mood.
Swallows over the fountain. Little commas in the sky.
The palms are combing the light. Very tidy palms.
I wrote Margot a letter from this bench once. She said yes.
That house has a new window box. Petunias. Well chosen.
The tiles under my feet have little shells pressed in. I love that.
Pull up a corner of bench. There is always room for one more.
The sky is doing peach now. Next comes rosé, Lucie says.
Odile has told me three nice things already. She keeps count.
My cane has a new rubber tip. We walk very quietly now.
Evenings like this, I forgive the hill for being steep.
Léo says the fountain fish is called Paul. Good evening, Paul.
A bench with a view is a sofa with ambition.
The light comes down the hill the same way I do. Slowly.
Time to sit. Time is very generous this time of day.
Margot will ring the bell for supper at nine. I will hear it.
Dinner is soup. Soup can wait for a sunset.
A good evening needs a bench, a hat and a little patience.
The church end of town says hello to the sea end.
I walked down with the light behind me. It pushed a little.
Grandchildren on Sunday, sunset on weekdays. Full calendar.
There is gold on the café windows. Free of charge.
Even the shadows are in a good mood this evening.
My grandmother said: sit facing the sea, the rest will follow.
I came down for the view. The view came up to meet me.
Somebody is grilling sardines up the lane. Six o'clock smells right.
Margot is making ratatouille. I can smell it from here, nearly.
A paper cone of roasted almonds. Still warm. Don't tell the doctor.
Basil on the café tables. Marcel rubs a leaf for luck.
The bakery has one baguette left. I have my eye on it.
Hear that? Ice in a glass. The café has started the evening.
Garlic and rosemary from the blue house. Lamb, I would say.
Fig season. My pocket has two, a bit squashed. Still lovely.
Cicadas are winding down. They work the afternoon shift.
A spoon on a saucer, somewhere behind me. Very civilised sound.
The sea air has a little salt in it. Like a good butter.
Lemonade from the kiosk. Sour first, then kind.
Pastis on the café terrace. It goes cloudy, like a little sky.
The stones of the promenade still hold the day's heat. Cosy.
Hot bread and cut grass. The town's two best perfumes.
Marcel's olives have rosemary on them. I can tell from the bench.
A fat bee on the lavender. Doing the last round of the day.
Apricot tart in the café window. I visit it like a museum.
Cheese, bread, a pear. Supper in my coat pocket. Ingenious.
The palm fronds rustle like someone turning a newspaper.
Thyme grows in the cracks by the steps. I step on it on purpose.
Coffee after five keeps me up. So I smell Marcel's instead.
My hat brim smells of sunshine. Forty summers of it.
The fountain drips on the bowl rim. Tick, tick. A wet clock.
Bouillabaisse at the café on Fridays. I plan my week around it.
A crêpe with sugar and lemon. My one weakness. Also honey.
The sparrows know the café drops crusts at six. Punctual birds.
A gravel crunch, then a cane tap. That's how you hear me coming.
Melon tonight. Margot taps them to choose. Like a doctor.
The jasmine on the wall opens in the evening. Shy flower.
Clatter of plates being set inside. Supper is rehearsing.
Bread, butter, radishes. Nobody needs a recipe for happiness.
Oranges on the kiosk counter, piled like little suns.
A whiff of pine from the hill. The trees are warm too.
Eggs being whisked by an open window. Omelette weather.
Paper bags crinkle at the bakery door. The last batch went out.
Mint tea, Yusuf promised. He makes it very sweet.
My granddaughter likes pistachio ice cream. Green as the shutters.
The breeze brought cinnamon. Somebody is spoiling a grandchild.
Chairs scraping on the terrace. The best kind of noise.
A good tomato smells like its leaves. Margot taught me that.
Bubbles of the fountain sound like a pot coming to the boil.
Some evenings I hear a radio playing old songs. Tonight, yes.
The cypresses smell green when the sun warms them. Hard to explain.
A cork popped at the café. Applause from a table. Lovely.
Soft cheese and honey. Margot says it is dessert. I say supper.
Lavender in my buttonhole. Margot's idea. A good idea.
The bench has a groove where my elbow goes. We fit.
Somebody's cat is purring on the wall behind me. Like a little engine.
Watermelon at the kiosk, sliced to order. Pink as the sky later.
Every step on the tiles sounds different. Henri shuffles. Léo gallops.
Sea breeze, warm stone, coffee. My three favourite smells, in order.
Socca in a paper sheet, black pepper on top. That is a dinner.
The newspaper is warm. I could toast bread on it.
Parsley being chopped somewhere. That neat little knock-knock.
Margot's tapenade is famous on our street. Two jars a week.
I hear the fountain, the gulls and a spoon. A small orchestra.
Blackberries from the lane behind the church. Purple fingers.
A bag of cherries and a bench. Spit the stones into the hedge.
The lime tree is in flower. It smells of honey and my youth.
Marcel's tarte tatin has a dark top. That's where the joy is.
The plaster on that wall is rough and warm. Like an old dog.
Pétanque balls clacking somewhere behind the church. Good game.
Crisp fried squid in a paper cone. Lemon squeezed on top. Bliss.
Fennel grows wild by the steps. Liquorice, if you crush it.
Nuts, raisins and a square of chocolate. My evening rations.
Bread crust is the best part. Anouk eats the middle. Teamwork.
Grilled peppers up the hill. Margot will want to know whose.
Café chairs have warm metal seats now. Sit quickly, then sigh.
A bottle of fizzy water. Very small fireworks on my tongue.
The light smells of dry grass. My grandfather said hay-gold.
Fresh goat cheese from the market. Margot hides it. I find it.
A hum from the string lights' wires. Warming up their voices.
Someone has a pot of mussels going. Wine, garlic, joy.
Zucchini flowers, stuffed and fried. Margot's Saturday special.
Bonsoir to the bakery girl. She waved with a loaf. Elegant.
Cold grapes from the icebox. The best invention since benches.
A slice of pain d'épices for the walk. Honey and spice, all the way.
The hill smells of rosemary on the way down. I brush past on purpose.
Supper is tomatoes and good bread. The view is the starter.
Whoever bakes on Rue Haute, thank you. My nose is grateful.
Strawberries from the market, warm from the sun. Better than sugar.
The swifts scream, the fountain hums. Evening has a soundtrack.
Milk bread for breakfast tomorrow. I bought it now to be sure.
Noon by the church bell. Noon by my stomach. They agree.
Marguerite sent me for one baguette. I may come home with two.
The fountain has been saying the same thing for sixty years. Kindly.
Blue shutters on the left, green on the right. Both correct.
I counted the awnings once. Eleven. I count them again for fun.
The clock is four minutes fast. We let it. It is keen.
Down the church steps, slowly. Thirty-two. Same as last year.
That roof tile has been crooked since 1979. It suits it.
A little stroll before lunch. Lunch will wait. It always does.
My granddaughter calls this hill a mountain. It is a good hill.
The bakery queue moves like a polite parade.
The awning on the café is new. Same stripes. Very sensible.
One more lap of the square. Then soup. Then a nap.
Noon, and the shadows have tucked themselves under the hats.
The bread is still warm. I am carrying it like a cat.
When I was a boy, the fountain was my ocean.
My father walked this route with this exact speed. I inherited it.
Someone painted the bench by the kiosk. I approve of the yellow.
Every shutter in town is open at noon. The houses are yawning.
The pigeons know my pocket has crumbs. Clever birds.
I tip my hat to the clock. It does not tip back. Still friends.
Marguerite and I danced by that fountain. 1968. Still dancing.
Henri walks faster than me. He claims it is the hat.
Fresh basil on a windowsill. Somebody is making a good lunch.
My cane knows every cobble. It taps hello to each one.
The church bell rings twelve. I always count along, in case.
Out for bread, and somehow I have a lemon. How did that happen?
Look at the light on those white walls. Like fresh milk.
